samples.summary: Staleness is patched only on the replace path; the displayed match set/highlights/counter and next/previous still operate on stale results, so Replace can act on a different occurrence than the one highlighted
samples.evidence: `FindReplaceState` never observes document changes. The diff adds `this.search(this.query, this.options)` at the top of `replaceActive` (line 63) and `replaceAll` (line 86), but `matches`/`activeIndex` are still stale for everything else: `packages/frontend/src/app/docs/docs-find-bar.tsx` only calls `syncHighlights()` after a user-initiated search/next/previous/replace, so after the user types in the document the highlight overlay and the "N of M" counter keep showing pre-edit offsets and `next()`/`previous()` still cycle the stale array. Worse for the stated outcome: the internal re-search keeps `prevIndex` when still in range (`search()`, lines 29-31), so the index that survives can now point at a *different* occurrence than the one the user sees highlighted — Replace then edits text the user did not select. The root fix belongs where the state is kept in sync with the doc (re-search on document change / version stamp), not only at the two write entry points.

samples.summary: Call sites still gate on stale match data before the new in-model re-search, so the fix is bypassed in the opposite direction
samples.evidence: `handleReplace` returns early when `state.activeIndex < 0` (line 134) and `handleReplaceAll` when `state.matches.length === 0` (line 143); the Replace/All buttons are also `disabled={matchCount === 0}` (lines 301, 308). Those checks read the stale snapshot the diff is trying to fix. If the user edits the document so that matches now exist (or an existing active index was cleared), the UI refuses to call into `FindReplaceState` at all and the newly-added re-search never runs. Placing the refresh inside the two model methods leaves the guarding layer working from data the model itself no longer trusts — the halves of the invariant live in two places.

Consolidating the 'refresh matches' behaviour in one place (or exposing a safe `refresh()`) would avoid two answers to the same question.

finding.summary: Staleness is patched only on the replace path; the displayed match set/highlights/counter and next/previous still operate on stale results, so Replace can act on a different occurrence than the one highlighted
finding.evidence: `FindReplaceState` never observes document changes. The diff adds `this.search(this.query, this.options)` at the top of `replaceActive` (line 63) and `replaceAll` (line 86), but `matches`/`activeIndex` are still stale for everything else: `packages/frontend/src/app/docs/docs-find-bar.tsx` only calls `syncHighlights()` after a user-initiated search/next/previous/replace, so after the user types in the document the highlight overlay and the "N of M" counter keep showing pre-edit offsets and `next()`/`previous()` still cycle the stale array. Worse for the stated outcome: the internal re-search keeps `prevIndex` when still in range (`search()`, lines 29-31), so the index that survives can now point at a *different* occurrence than the one the user sees highlighted — Replace then edits text the user did not select. verdict.reason: The finding's evidence holds up on inspection. `FindReplaceState` (packages/docs/src/view/find-replace.ts:8-35) has no document-change observation: its constructor takes only `doc` and `snapshot`, and `search()` preserves `prevIndex` whenever it is still within range of the freshly recomputed array (lines 29-31), so a surviving index can address a different occurrence than the one the user saw highlighted. The re-search guard exists only at the two write entry points, `replaceActive` (line 63) and `replaceAll` (line 86). On the frontend, `docs-find-bar.tsx` calls `syncHighlights()` only from `runSearch` (line 96), `handleNext` (116), `handlePrevious` (123), `handleReplace` (137) and `handleReplaceAll` (146); none of its `useEffect`s subscribe to document changes, so matches/counter/next/previous stay stale after the user types. The editor side confirms there is no compensating invalidation: `editor.ts:1490-1491` holds `searchMatches`/`activeMatchIndex` as-is, renders highlights from them at 2114-2118, and clears them only in `clearSearchMatches` (4206-4218) — no edit path resets or remaps them. The accompanying tests (packages/docs/test/view/find-replace.test.ts:67, 85) cover only the replace path, corroborating the scoped fix. No refutation ground applies: the code is present as described, nothing guards the stale path, and the claim (fix applied at the wrong layer, leaving the stated outcome unmet for the user) is within the design-fit lane. I could not retrieve the originating issue's acceptance text to establish that highlight/counter staleness was explicitly out of scope, so the uncertainty keeps the finding.

verdict.reason: The quoted guards do exist (docs-find-bar.tsx:134, :143, :301, :308), but they do not bypass the fix and are not blocking under the design-fit rubric. The diff's targeted scenario — search succeeds, user edits the document, user hits Replace — passes every guard: after a successful search `syncHighlights` (docs-find-bar.tsx:77-83) sets `matchCount > 0` and `state.activeIndex >= 0`, and nothing resets them on document mutation (the FindReplaceState rebuild effect at :60-69 keys on `editor`, which docs-view.tsx:681-685 passes as the stable `mountedEditor`). So the newly added re-search at find-replace.ts:63 and :86 does run, exactly as the new tests at find-replace.test.ts:67-101 model. The only case the guards block is when the last known match set was empty, where they refuse a write rather than permit a wrong-offset one — fail-safe, and identical staleness already governs Previous/Next (:252, :265) and the "No results" counter (:183), i.e. a pre-existing "find bar does not observe document mutations" UX gap orthogonal to the stale-offset corruption being fixed. Under this lens that leaves a duplicated guard across the UI/model boundary whose cost stays inside the codebase's own tidiness: `minor`, which never blocks. No acceptance criterion is left unmet, no divergent-answers data problem, no Non-Goal breached.
